idiom_name: algebra as a plain object of closures; interpreter injected as a parameter
implementation_notes: JavaScript needs no type-level machinery at all: the algebra is an object literal of functions over the interpreted value, the program is a function taking that object, and every interpreter is another object; swapping meaning is passing a different argument. What replaces the classic structure: the type-class instance becomes an ordinary value and the program's 'polymorphism' becomes a parameter - there is no F to quantify over, so an effectful interpreter simply returns promises or IO values and the effect is fixed at the call site. The encoding is justified whenever a JS module must produce the same result in several ways (render, log, record, stub) and the typed variant is unavailable; there is no reason to add a wrapper layer beyond that.
pitfalls: There are no static types, so the algebra contract is documentation: a typo in a method name fails at the first call with a TypeError, and a partially implemented interpreter fails only when the missing operation is reached.

Mixing synchronous and asynchronous interpreters changes the program's shape (the result becomes a promise), so a dictionary cannot be swapped freely between the two - keep all interpreters of one algebra on the same side.
Module-level interpreter singletons make the choice global and order-dependent; pass the dictionary in, or tests leak state into each other.
Closures capture their environment by reference: an interpreter that closes over mutable state behaves differently per call site - keep interpreter state explicit.
